takes.text: You tap a box that says you're not a robot.
Researchers say the test started before your finger got there.
For years, the test was reading wobbly letters.
In twenty thirteen, Google said its risk analysis covers everything you do around a challenge, not only the answer you type.
In twenty fourteen, the checkbox arrived, and many people passed with one click.
The click feels like the test. It's really a request for a verdict.
The evidence was gathered around it. If it looks human, you pass. If it can't tell, you get a puzzle.
So what does it watch? Google doesn't publish the full list.
A twenty twenty-one survey describes the checkbox recording cursor movement, where you click, and how long the pointer hovers.
It also records browser details and cookies. Google's own FAQ calls a cookie essential to that analysis.
A real hand never moves at one steady speed.
It speeds up, peaks, and eases into the target.
In nineteen eighty-five, Flash and Hogan modeled arm movement this way: a smooth, bell-shaped curve of speed.
One published detector checks cursor paths against a model like that.
In a twenty twenty-four study of reCAPTCHA version two, any cursor movement cut the number of puzzles needed to pass.
Straight paths and curved ones were not significantly different.
So is it the wobble? Google doesn't say.
Then there's the browser.
A twenty twenty-four study reports that cookies and browsing history carry substantial weight in whether a visitor seems human.
Browsing history is what researchers report. Google hasn't confirmed it.
Version three has no checkbox at all.
It returns a score from zero to one. One means very likely a good interaction. Zero means very likely a bot.
Each site sets its own cutoff, and Google suggests starting at point five.
But a score can be pushed. In twenty nineteen, researchers trained an AI agent to move and click in a simulator they built.
It reached a score of point nine about ninety-seven percent of the time. The simulator isn't the live site.
A twenty twenty-three study ran for thirteen months with more than thirty-six hundred people.
Its authors judged the checkbox costly, with close to no security gain, and say it should be retired.
Nobody outside Google knows how the signals are weighted. So every study tests from the outside.
So the tap is the last step, not the test.
It cares how you got there.
